clue.text: Puts one's hands together audibly to applaud

indicators.note: audibly says the words before it are to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: someone at prayer puts their palms together

explanation.surface: A crowd claps its hands to show approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The hands go together in prayer, not in clapping, though the surface wants applause.
explanation.definitionFit: To praise someone is to commend or acclaim them, which is what applause does.

clue.text: Bear bleating sound from pompous official

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, the famous bear of A. A. Milne

explanation.surface: A grumbling bear makes a scornful noise at some self-important functionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Pooh-Bah is the haughty holder of many offices in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the Mikado character became a general term for a self-important person holding high office.

clue.text: Athenian upper chamber

definitions.meaning: first meaning: belonging to Attica, the region around Athens
second meaning: a room just under the roof

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek parliamentary house sitting above another.
explanation.walkthrough: Upper chamber suggests a senate, but here it is simply a room at the top of a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic Greek is the dialect of Athens, and a loft room under the roof is also called this.

clue.text: Aliens by the way, eleven in Glasgow

parts.note: a football team of eleven based in Glasgow

explanation.surface: An aside noting that some foreigners are a Scottish football side.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is one of Glasgow's two big football clubs; a football side has eleven players.
explanation.definitionFit: Aliens are people from elsewhere, unknown to the locals, so outsiders or newcomers.

clue.text: Charges a charge, say?

indicators.note: say tells us to speak the phrase before it and listen to how it comes out

parts.note: a tax is a charge levied by the state

explanation.surface: A puzzle about whether a fee counts as one charge or several.
explanation.walkthrough: Charges is the military sense, rushing at an enemy; a charge is a financial one, a levy.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge is to rush at an enemy in assault, so charges are assaults or onslaughts.

clue.text: One feels number getting squeezed by girl

indicators.note: something squeezed is held tight between two sides, so it goes inside the girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone feels for a statistic being squeezed by a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Number is the plain numeral, not the anaesthetic sense of numb.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect's feeler is the thing it uses to sense its surroundings by touch.

clue.text: Tiger (if revolutionary) inverts a capital T

definitions.note: the answer names the people; a revolutionary member of it was a Tamil Tiger

indicators.note: to invert is to turn upside down, so in a down light the letters run the other way

parts.note: Lima is the capital of Peru

explanation.surface: A rebel tiger turns a capital letter T upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tamil Tigers were the Sri Lankan separatist rebels; a capital here is a city, not a capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tamil Tigers were a rebel movement, so a Tamil who took up revolution would be one of the Tigers.

clue.text: Artist's "Boy in Blue"?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: John ..., English landscape painter
second meaning: a policeman, from the blue uniform

explanation.surface: The title of a painting, like Gainsborough's Blue Boy.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like a painting's title; boys in blue is slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable painted The Hay Wain; a constable is also the lowest rank of British police officer.

clue.text: 's not warm, we hear, for many fish

indicators.note: we hear says the words are to be judged by their sound when spoken

parts.note: not warm is cool, after the 's

explanation.surface: A fragment of chatter about the chilly water a shoal swims in.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue starts with a stray 's, which must be read as part of the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A large group of fish swimming together is called a shoal or by this collective noun.

clue.text: Bird moving out with Billy?

indicators.note: moving says the letters of the next word shift into a new order

parts.note: a billycan is a camping pot, so billy is a can

explanation.surface: A bird flies off accompanied by a goat or a lad named Billy.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark nods to the bird's enormous bill.
explanation.definitionFit: The toucan is a tropical American bird famous for its huge colourful beak.

clue.text: Order more stout and that's the limit

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, the furthest out

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the next letters are set out afresh

explanation.surface: A drinker calls for another pint of stout, and the barman says that is enough.
explanation.walkthrough: Order looks like a request at the bar but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at the very limit lies farthest from the centre, at the extreme edge.

clue.text: Artist to eat …

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Edvard ..., Norwegian painter of The Scream

explanation.surface: A painter about to have a meal, continued in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, where the breakfast arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: Edvard Munch painted The Scream; the same word means to chew food steadily and audibly.

clue.text: … another for breakfast?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: another painter, carrying on from the previous clue
second meaning: a cured pork food eaten at breakfast

explanation.surface: Read with the clue before, a painter eats a second painter for breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: Another leans on the previous clue's Artist: Francis Bacon was an Irish-born British painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon painted screaming popes, and cured pork rashers are a staple of a cooked morning meal.

clue.text: Artist can drink rum tot

indicators.note: rum means odd or strange, so the following word comes out in an odd order

explanation.surface: A painter who can knock back a tot of rum.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum looks like the drink but is the anagram signal; drink is the ale.
explanation.definitionFit: Canaletto was the Venetian painter famous for his detailed views of Venice's canals.

clue.text: Artist not entirely devout, being without godhead

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is taken short of its full length
without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the head, or first letter, of god

explanation.surface: A painter who is only half-religious and lives without a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: Godhead looks like divinity but is just the first letter of god.
explanation.definitionFit: Hans Holbein the Younger was the German-born court painter to Henry VIII of England.

clue.text: Girl with tie on loosely hanging about

indicators.note: loosely says the letters are not fixed in place and may be rearranged

explanation.surface: A young woman wearing a tie that hangs slack.
explanation.walkthrough: Hanging about seems to describe the loose tie but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanging about means lingering idly with no clear purpose, a synonym for this word.

clue.text: With hands on hips, king in the end gets the whiff of armpits

indicators.note: in places the monarch's letter inside the word for end

parts.note: an end is a goal or aim

explanation.surface: A monarch stands with hands on hips and catches a smell of sweat.
explanation.walkthrough: BO is body odour; with arms akimbo the armpits are exposed, adding to the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes standing with hands on the hips and elbows turned outwards.

clue.text: Put one's oar in and take one's tripe out

indicators.note: out suggests the words are turned out of their order

parts.note: fodder for rearranging, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Interfering in a conversation, then removing the offal from a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Tripe is stomach lining, and talking tripe means nonsense, which fits the interfering talker.
explanation.definitionFit: To put one's oar in is to intervene uninvited, which is to interrupt or interject.

clue.text: Artist's advice to angler having caught a minnow?

parts.words: advice to angler having caught a minnow
parts.note: a minnow is too small to keep, so the advice is to throw it back

explanation.surface: A painter tells a fisherman to throw back a tiny catch.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal is unsignalled: the advice, read from the end, gives the painter. James Tissot was a French painter of Victorian society.
explanation.definitionFit: James Tissot was a nineteenth-century French painter who worked in London painting fashionable society scenes.

clue.text: Artist to draw game

parts.note: a drawn match is a tie

explanation.surface: A painter about to sketch a sporting match.
explanation.walkthrough: Draw is the result of a match, not sketching.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was the Venetian painter of grand ceiling frescoes in the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Bone in spuds in shreds

indicators.note: in puts the bone's letter inside the word for potatoes

explanation.surface: A bone found in mashed potatoes that has been torn to bits.
explanation.walkthrough: Spuds and taters are both slang for potatoes; in shreds and in tatters mean the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatters are torn ragged pieces, especially of cloth, the same as shreds.

clue.text: Artist's "Colossus" I framed

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so the giant's name goes round the letter

explanation.surface: A painter claims a giant painting called Colossus and boasts of framing it.
explanation.walkthrough: Framed fits the painting picture neatly, but it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian was the great Venetian Renaissance painter, known for his rich use of colour.

clue.text: Shows contempt for its past performance

indicators.note: a performance is a reworking, so the letters are presented in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a bygone show of theirs.
explanation.walkthrough: Performance reads as a noun in the surface but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To spit at someone is a gesture of scorn, so the phrase means showing disdain towards them.

clue.text: Piece that is for a beginner

explanation.surface: Advice on which chess piece suits a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: Piece suggests a chess or game piece in the surface, and that is the meaning used.
explanation.definitionFit: A rookie is a novice or new recruit, someone just starting out.

clue.text: Not immediately after the alarm was raised?

definitions.text: Not immediately after the alarm was raised?

parts.words: Not immediately after the alarm was raised?
parts.note: surface reading: someone slow to respond to a warning or emergency
setter's reading: the alarm clock went off and the sleeper failed to get up in time

explanation.surface: Someone delayed in reacting when a warning was sounded.
explanation.walkthrough: Raising the alarm suggests an emergency; the alarm is a clock, and the late riser stayed in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To have slept past the intended waking time is to have stayed asleep too long.

clue.text: French composer's irony's not right

indicators.note: not means without, so a letter is taken away

explanation.surface: A French composer's sarcasm misses the mark.
explanation.walkthrough: Erik Satie wrote the Gymnopédies.
explanation.definitionFit: Erik Satie was a French composer of quirky piano pieces such as the Gymnopédies.

clue.text: Two from the centre: if eleven were ten would broadcast

indicators.note: if one thing were another, the second takes the first's place

parts.note: ten written as figures 1 0 looks like I O
eleven written as figures 1 1 looks like I I

explanation.surface: A riddle about numbers and a broadcast, set against two lines from a centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the answer's last two letters as figures and they read 11; change them to 10 and you get the broadcasting word.
explanation.definitionFit: Radii are the lines from the middle of a circle to its edge; two of them form a plural.

clue.text: With going more firm, jockey's heart goes to his head

definitions.note: of a racecourse, firmer going means less wet

indicators.note: the middle letter moves up to the front, a one-letter shift in the order

parts.note: a jockey is a rider; his heart is the middle letter

explanation.surface: A jockey's courage rises as the racecourse ground hardens.
explanation.walkthrough: Going is the racing word for the state of the ground; take the middle letter of the jockey word and put it first.
explanation.definitionFit: Firmer going on a racecourse is ground that has less moisture in it, so less wet.

clue.text: Artist needs reclining model to draw off

indicators.note: reclining means lying back, so the following words are read backwards

parts.note: to milk is to draw off liquid

explanation.surface: A painter needs a model lying down to draw from.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustav Klimt painted The Kiss; model to draw fits a life class, but each word works alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Klimt was the Austrian painter of The Kiss, famous for his gold-leaf works.

clue.text: Cad wears glasses or is disguised for religious works

indicators.note: something worn goes round the wearer, so the glasses surround the cad

parts.note: a pair of lenses look like two O's

indicators.note: disguised means made to look different, so those letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cad puts on spectacles as a disguise for church work.
explanation.walkthrough: OO is the crossword picture of a pair of spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: These are large musical works for voices and orchestra on sacred subjects, like Handel's Messiah.

clue.text: Artist's marbles missing in some records

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the following word is dropped from the marbles

parts.note: the Elgin Marbles in the British Museum

indicators.note: some means only part, so the word that follows is cut short

explanation.surface: An artist has lost his marbles, according to some archives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Elgin Marbles are Greek sculptures in the British Museum; losing one's marbles also means going mad.
explanation.definitionFit: El Greco was the Cretan-born painter who worked in Toledo, Spain, known for elongated figures.

clue.text: Artist forged art? Sue!

indicators.note: forged means faked or hammered into shape, so the letters are remade

explanation.surface: Someone is told to take a painter to court for faking art.
explanation.walkthrough: Georges Seurat was the French pointillist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Georges Seurat was the French painter who pioneered pointillism, painting with tiny dots of colour.
